The Face, Scalp & Temporal Fossa

A complete study companion covering the anatomy of the face, the muscles of facial expression, the sensory and motor innervation of the face, the blood supply of the face, the temporal fossa, and the five layers of the scalp (SCALP).

Lecture Roadmap

This session covers three regions of the head, moving from anterior to lateral to superior:

1) The Face

Definition · muscles of facial expression · motor & sensory innervation · blood supply

2) Temporal Fossa

Location · shape · boundaries · floor & roof · contents

3) The Scalp

Five layers — remembered by the mnemonic SCALP

Learning objectives

  • Define the boundaries of the face and describe the general architecture of the muscles of facial expression.
  • List the muscles of facial expression by region (scalp, orbit, nose, mouth, ear) and state their actions.
  • Describe the course and five terminal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII), the motor supply to the face.
  • Describe the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) as the sensory supply to the face.
  • Describe the arterial supply (facial and transverse facial arteries) and venous drainage of the face.
  • Describe the location, shape, boundaries, floor, roof, and contents of the temporal fossa.
  • List the five layers of the scalp and describe the clinically important properties of each layer.
1

Definition of the Face

The face is the anterior aspect of the head.

  • Superior–inferior extent: from the forehead (hairline) down to the chin.
  • Side-to-side extent: from one ear to the other.
2

Muscles of Facial Expression

Introduction · Function · Innervation

General organisation

The muscles of facial expression are skeletal (voluntary) muscles — one of the three muscle types in the body alongside cardiac muscle (heart) and smooth muscle (found in hollow viscera such as the uterus, rectum and vagina). Skeletal muscle shares the striated appearance of cardiac muscle.

  • They lie within the superficial fascia of the face and scalp.
  • Their origin is from either bone or fascia.
  • Their insertion is into the skin.
Key exception to remember: Unlike the muscles of the limbs, which typically attach bone-to-bone or bone-to-cartilage via tendons (e.g. the three muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm — coracobrachialis, brachialis and biceps brachii — insert onto bone, with only partial fascial attachment), the muscles of facial expression insert directly into the skin or superficial fascia. This is what allows their contraction to move the skin itself and produce facial expressions, rather than moving a joint.

Because these muscles control expression, they are also called the "muscles of facial expression."

Occipitofrontalis Scalp / forehead

A single muscle with two bellies connected by an aponeurosis:

  • Frontal belly (frontalis) — anterior, over the forehead.
  • Occipital belly (occipitalis) — posterior, over the back of the skull.
  • The two bellies are joined by the epicranial aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica) — this aponeurosis is also the third layer of the scalp (see SCALP mnemonic below).

Orbicularis oculi & Corrugator supercilii Eye

MusclePartsAction
Orbicularis oculiOrbital part & palpebral partCloses and opens the eye (sphincter of the orbit)
Corrugator supercilii—Draws the eyebrows together/downward — produces the vertical frown ("wrinkling") lines between the eyebrows

Nasalis & Procerus Nose

MusclePartsAction
NasalisTransverse part (across the bridge of the nose) & alar partOpens and closes the nostrils (nares/nostril = external orifices of the nose)
Procerus—Wrinkles the skin over the bridge of the nose; assists corrugator supercilii in frowning

Orbicularis oris Mouth

A circular (sphincter-like) muscle that surrounds the mouth and forms the substance of the upper and lower lips, together with skin, mucous membrane, lymphatics, and blood vessels. Many other facial muscles converge and blend into orbicularis oris, contributing to the lips.

Action: controls dilatation and constriction of the oral fissure (the anterior opening/entrance of the mouth).

Buccinator Cheek

High-yield: The parotid duct (duct of the parotid salivary gland) pierces the buccinator muscle to open into the oral cavity.

Zygomaticus & Levator group Cheek / upper lip

MuscleAttachment / notesAction
Zygomaticus majorLarger of the two; attaches to the zygomatic boneElevates the angle of the mouth (smiling); contributes to the prominence of the cheek
Zygomaticus minorSmaller companion muscle; also attaches to the zygomatic boneAssists in elevating the upper lip
Levator labii superiorisSome texts describe it as one muscle with the next; others separate it into two distinct musclesElevates ("raises") the upper lip — dilates the oral fissure
Levator labii superioris alaeque nasi—Elevates the upper lip and the ala of the nose
Levator anguli orisLies at the angle of the mouthElevates the angle of the mouth

Depressor group, Mentalis, Risorius & Platysma Lower lip / chin / neck

MuscleAction
Depressor anguli orisPulls the angle of the mouth downward (opposes levator anguli oris)
Depressor labii inferiorisPulls the lower lip downward
MentalisWrinkles the skin over the chin
RisoriusPulls the angle of the mouth laterally — contributes to smiling
PlatysmaThin sheet in the superficial fascia of the neck, continuous with the muscles of facial expression

Auricular Muscles Ear

MusclePositionAction
Superior auricularAbove the auricle (external ear)Raises the ear
Anterior auricularIn front of the auricleDraws the ear forward
Posterior auricularBehind the auricleDraws the ear backward
Clinical/anatomical curiosity: A small proportion of people retain the vestigial ability to voluntarily contract the auricular muscles and move their ears — up, forward, or backward.

Levator palpebrae superioris Eyelid

Like any skeletal muscle, it is grossly composed of a fleshy part (muscle belly) and a tendinous part (tendon). It elevates (raises) the upper eyelid, opening the eye.

Important exception: Although this muscle helps open the eye and sits in the orbit alongside the facial muscles, it is a striated muscle derived differently from the rest of facial expression muscles — classically it is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (CN III), not the facial nerve. Keep this exception in mind, since exam questions on "innervation of muscles that open/close the eye" often test the contrast between orbicularis oculi (facial nerve) and levator palpebrae superioris (oculomotor nerve).

Function of the muscles of facial expression

As a group, the muscles of facial expression act as sphincters and dilators of the orifices of the face — the orbits (eyes), the nose, and the mouth. They contract either to open these orifices (dilators) or to close them (sphincters/constrictors).

Innervation of the muscles of facial expression

All the muscles of facial expression are supplied by a single nerve: the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).

High-yield: The facial nerve arises from the brainstem specifically at the pons (not the midbrain, and not the medulla).

For orientation: the trochlear (IV) and oculomotor (III) nerves arise from the midbrain; the facial (VII), vestibulocochlear (VIII) and trigeminal (V) nerves arise from the pons; the glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), spinal accessory (XI) and hypoglossal (XII) nerves arise from the medulla oblongata.

Course of the facial nerve

  • The facial nerve passes within the substance of the parotid gland.
  • It emerges from the anterior border of the parotid gland and then divides into five terminal branches.
BranchCourse / distribution
TemporalUppermost branch, courses over the temple
ZygomaticRuns towards the zygomatic bone
BuccalRuns across the middle of the face (cheek)
Marginal mandibularRuns down along the mandible
CervicalDescends into the neck / upper part of the chest wall (supplies platysma)
Mnemonic (5 branches, top to bottom): "Ten Zebras Bit My Cat" → Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical.
3

Blood Supply of the Face

Arterial supply

  • The main artery is the facial artery, a branch of the external carotid artery.
  • A second contributor is the transverse facial artery, a branch of the superficial temporal artery (itself a branch of the external carotid artery); it helps the facial artery supply the face.

Course of the facial artery

Arises from the external carotid artery → runs to the lower border of the mandible → curves below the submandibular gland → ascends to reach the angle of the mouth → gives branches that supply the whole face.

Venous drainage

Venous drainage of the face is via the facial vein.

4

Sensory Innervation of the Face

Sensation is carried from the face by the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V), which gives three branches to the face (tri- = three):

  1. Ophthalmic nerve (V1)
  2. Maxillary nerve (V2)
  3. Mandibular nerve (V3)

All three divisions arise from the trigeminal ganglion — a peripheral (sensory) ganglion associated with this cranial nerve, part of the peripheral nervous system. The mandibular division passes into the infratemporal fossa. Together, the three divisions provide sensory innervation to the entire face.

High-yield summary — Face innervation at a glance:
ModalityNerveOrigin
Motor (muscles of facial expression)Facial nerve (CN VII)Pons
Sensory (skin of the face)Trigeminal nerve (CN V) — ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular divisionsPons
5

Temporal Fossa

Location · Shape · Boundaries · Floor · Roof · Contents

The region overlying this fossa — the lateral side of the head — is called the temple.

Location

The temporal fossa covers the lateral surface of the skull. If the temporal fascia and temporalis muscle (which form its roof) are removed, an actual depression/fossa is revealed underneath.

Shape

A narrow, fan-shaped space.

Boundaries

DirectionBoundary
Superior & posteriorThe temporal lines (superior and inferior temporal lines)
LateralThe temporal fascia and the zygomatic arch
AnteriorThe frontal bone and the zygomatic bone
InferiorThe infratemporal crest (separates the temporal fossa above from the infratemporal fossa below)

Floor & Roof

Note the orientation: unlike a typical "floor," the floor of the temporal fossa lies on the side of the skull, not underneath it.

StructureFormed by
FloorParts of four bones: frontal (anteriorly), greater wing of the sphenoid (directly behind the frontal bone), temporal bone (posteriorly), and parietal bone (superiorly)
RoofThe temporal fascia
Clinical correlation: The junction of these four bones forming the floor (frontal, parietal, temporal, greater wing of sphenoid) corresponds to the region known as the pterion — the thinnest part of the lateral skull and a clinically important landmark, as it overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery and is vulnerable to fracture.

Contents

The roof-forming temporal fascia is itself also listed among the contents, together with the following six structures (in two pairs and two singles):

ContentSource / notes
Temporalis muscleThe chief muscle occupying the fossa
Temporal fasciaForms the roof and is also a content
Deep temporal nerves (2)Branches of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve
Zygomaticotemporal nerve (1)—
Deep temporal arteries (2)Branches of the maxillary artery
Middle temporal artery (1)Branch of the superficial temporal artery
Grouping trick: Contents come in pairs — 2 deep temporal nerves + 2 deep temporal arteries — plus 2 single structures on each side (zygomaticotemporal nerve; middle temporal artery), plus the muscle and fascia.
6

The Scalp

Structure in the form of five layers
Mnemonic — SCALP (five layers, superficial to deep):
LetterLayer
SSkin
CConnective tissue (dense)
AAponeurosis (epicranial aponeurosis / galea aponeurotica)
LLoose (areolar) connective tissue
PPericranium

1. Skin S

The outermost layer of the scalp. Structurally similar to skin elsewhere in the body, with the notable exception that hair is present in large amounts.

2. Connective tissue (dense) C

This layer anchors the skin to the third layer (the aponeurosis) and contains the arteries, veins and nerves supplying the scalp.

Clinical correlation: Because the blood vessels of the scalp are held within this dense connective tissue and cannot easily retract or collapse, scalp lacerations that cut through this layer tend to bleed profusely.

3. Aponeurosis (epicranial aponeurosis / galea aponeurotica) A

Firmly attached to the skin via the dense connective tissue of the second layer. This layer is formed by the occipitofrontalis muscle — its frontal bellies anteriorly and occipital bellies posteriorly, joined by this aponeurotic tendon.

4. Loose (areolar) connective tissue L

Separates the aponeurotic layer from the pericranium and facilitates movement of the scalp proper over the calvaria.

Clinical correlation: This layer is often called the "danger area" of the scalp — because it is loose and richly connected by emissary veins to the intracranial venous sinuses, infection or blood introduced here can spread widely across the scalp and potentially intracranially.

5. Pericranium P

The deepest layer of the scalp, lying directly in contact with the bones of the skull. It is the periosteum on the outer surface of the calvaria.

  • It is attached to the bones of the calvaria but is generally removable.
  • Exception — at the sutures: where the bones of the skull meet (forming fibrous joints called sutures), the pericranium is firmly attached, because it blends with the fibrous connective tissue of the suture joint.
★

High-Yield Exam Zone

High-Yield Exam Pearls

  • The parotid duct pierces the buccinator muscle to open into the oral cavity.
  • All muscles of facial expression are innervated by a single nerve: the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).
  • The facial nerve exits the brainstem specifically from the pons, not the midbrain or the medulla.
  • The trigeminal ganglion gives rise to three divisions — ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular — that carry sensory innervation from the face.
  • The floor of the temporal fossa is formed by parts of four bones: frontal, parietal, greater wing of the sphenoid, and temporal.
  • The letters of SCALP stand for its five layers: Skin, Connective tissue (dense), Aponeurosis, Loose connective tissue, and Pericranium.

Clinical Pearls

  • Muscle origin/insertion exception: unlike limb muscles which attach bone-to-bone or bone-to-cartilage, the muscles of facial expression often insert directly into the superficial fascia or skin — allowing them to pull the skin and create facial expressions.
  • Voluntary ear movement: some individuals retain the vestigial ability to voluntarily contract the auricular muscles (superior, anterior, posterior) to move their ears.
  • Vascularity of the scalp: in classic textbook diagrams, structures colored red indicate arteries, green indicates connective tissue, and yellow indicates nerves or fat. The dense connective tissue layer of the scalp heavily anchors the skin, which explains why scalp lacerations bleed profusely (vessels are held open within this layer).
  • Scalp mobility and infection spread: the loose areolar connective tissue (4th layer) facilitates movement of the scalp proper over the calvaria and is the plane along which infection/blood can spread widely ("danger area" of the scalp).
  • Pericranium adherence: the pericranium (periosteum) is generally removable from the skull bones, but is firmly attached at the sutures because it blends with the fibrous connective tissue of these joints.

Glossary of Difficult Terms

TermMeaning
AponeurosisA broad, flat sheet of tendon-like connective tissue connecting a muscle to the part it moves (here, connecting the two bellies of occipitofrontalis).
CalvariaThe dome-shaped upper part of the skull (skull cap).
SphincterA ring-like muscle that constricts/closes an orifice.
DilatorA muscle that opens/widens an orifice.
Oral fissureThe anterior opening (entrance) of the mouth.
Nares / nostrilsThe external openings of the nose.
AuricleThe visible external part of the ear (pinna).
SuturesFibrous joints between the bones of the skull.
PeriosteumThe dense connective tissue membrane covering the outer surface of bone (except at joint surfaces).
Infratemporal crestA bony ridge that separates the temporal fossa (above) from the infratemporal fossa (below).
Galea aponeuroticaAlternative name for the epicranial aponeurosis, the tendinous third layer of the scalp.
